paper_title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

Existing motion benchmarks share these assumptions, covering conventional skeletons with relatively simple instructions. Large language models (LLMs) offer way to handle such complex instructions, and current systems use them in three ways  (Table 1)  . common practice is to let the LLM split the instruction into segments for specialized motion generator; the result looks natural and is cheap to produce, but remains bound to the generators skeleton and coarse semantics. Another route has the LLM plan video, from which 3D motion is recovered and retargeted. Video models bring strong visual priors, but generation is expensive, recovery models are developed mainly for humans, and precise timing and amplitude are often lost along the way. The LLM can also write motion itself through spatiotemporal reasoning, which adapts to arbitrary structures and allows fine-grained control; however, frame-by-frame joint outputs consume many tokens and lack kinematic constraints. To compare these paradigms under diverse morphologies and complex instructions, we introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories: humanoid, multiped, axial, winged, mixed-limb, and mechanical. Its text instructions and numeric constraints require multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory control. The evaluation separates textual semantic compliance from program-verified numeric accuracy, and further assesses phase completeness, morphology fit, and animation quality. On this benchmark, we systematically analyze the control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs of the three paradigms. The comparison shows that direct agent-driven generation holds the most promise for cross-morphology adaptability and fine-grained control, but outputting every joint coordinate frame by frame is costly and difficult, and the lack of bone-length and contact constraints makes the motion prone to interpenetration and hard to control. We therefore propose an Agentic Motion Framework. The agent first divides the instruction into motion phases and timing, and then selects key parts and end-effectors and plans their trajectories and targets in each phase. Next, the executor obtains full-body poses through kinematic solving and corrects interpenetration and ground contact using the deformed mesh. Finally, the exported animation is validated. Because the agent writes only small set of semantic parameters, this pipeline reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy. Our contributions are as follows: We analyze complex instruction-driven motion generation for diverse 3D assets, task that requires multi-part coordination, multi-phase execution, and numeric control. And we summarize three common LLM-assisted paradigms. We propose DivDynBench, benchmark covering six morphology categories. It evaluates rigging and complex motion generation, using visual scoring and program verification to measure instruction compliance, phase completeness, morphology fit, and animation quality. We compare the three paradigms on this benchmark in terms of control, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation cost. Based on this, we design an Agentic Motion Framework that improves rigging and motion generation. 2. Related Works 2.1. 3D and 4D Generation 3D and 4D content generation has become an active research area. Early zero-shot training methods [21, 27, 35, 51] optimize individual assets with pretrained 2D diffusion priors, improving fidelity, diversity, and image-guided appearance control. Image-conditioned feed-forward reconstruction and editing methods [11, 26, 57] greatly reduce 2 per-asset generation time. Hunyuan3D 1.0 [46] combines multiview diffusion with feed-forward reconstruction for high-quality asset creation. Subsequent 3D generative models [40, 56] improve geometric detail and appearance, while approaches using 3D latent diffusion and sparse representations [37, 38] advance high-resolution shape generation. For dynamic content, 4D reconstruction methods [43, 45] recover scenes from multiview videos, achieving highfidelity, real-time novel-view synthesis and robust reconstruction under wide-range movements and scene changes. Diffusion-based generative methods [3, 23] synthesize dynamic assets, L4GM [24] enables feed-forward reconstruction from monocular video, and Animate3D [13] animates existing assets with multiview video diffusion. These advances improve visual quality and efficiency, but visual realism alone does not ensure execution of complex instructions involving coordinated parts, ordered phases, and precise motion constraints. 2.2. Agentic Generation To handle more complex and precise 3D and 4D generation requests, recent methods introduce language-model agents for planning, tool use, and iterative refinement. Holodeck [47] translates language into asset selection and spatial constraints for environment construction, and SceneCraft [12] generates Blender code from scene graphs and refines rendered scenes through visual feedback. Agentic 4D scene composition methods [41, 50] decompose multi-object scenes into trajectory-planned components and model geometry-aware temporal transitions between them. Beyond single-scene construction, world-model unified methods [5, 10, 20, 39, 52] combine agent planning, generation, and feedback to construct explorable 3D worlds and playable gaming worlds, argue for moving beyond injecting world knowledge into isolated tasks toward unified framework, and provide standardized codebases and definitions for such advanced world models. Recent coding models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 also demonstrate strong interactive 3D scene-building capabilities in reported AA-3D and professional-environment evaluations [2, 6, 7]. However, constructing visually rich dynamic scenes remains distinct from generating precise, instruction-following motion for avatars with diverse articulated structures. 2.3. Avatar Motion Generation Motion generation methods explore diffusion-based modeling [30] and discrete motion representations [9, 53]. Textmotion datasets [8, 48] support language-conditioned human and animal motion, while methods [15, 19, 32] extend generation across diverse skeletons. Automatic rigging methods [18, 42, 54] infer skeletons and skinning, while Puppeteer [25] connects rigging with video-guided animation. Neural Kinematic Networks [31] transfer motion across body proportions, and Skeleton-Aware Networks [1] support retargeting between different but homeomorphic skeletons. Agent-driven animators [49, 58] require pre-rigged or URDF-articulated assets and do not handle long multi-joint limbs. Despite these advances in control and skeletal coverage, reliably executing long-horizon, multi-part instructions on nonstandard skeletons remains challenging. Recent benchmarks [17, 44] examine instruction following and motion quality, while DivDynBench evaluates rigging and complex text/numeric motion across diverse morphologies. 3. DivDynBench DivDynBench follows common 3D asset import workflow: its inputs are readable GLB assets, rather than groundtruth motion clips on standardized human skeleton. We define rigging task starting from raw mesh and an instruction-driven motion task using either predicted rig or provided reference rig. 3.1. Asset Collection and Morphology Coverage To reflect practical user workflows, we collect outputs from 3D generative models, basic shapes downloaded directly from the internet, and assets from engine libraries. These cover humanoids, multipeds, axial bodies, winged creatures, mixed-limb characters, and articulated mechanical objects. Each asset is organized as self-contained GLB with manually designed skeleton and skinning weights as rigging ground truth. The 50 assets and their associated 850 motion tasks are shown in Fig. 2. Table 2 compares motion-generation case counts, morphology coverage, and task complexity. Evaluation Metrics We evaluate structural inference and motion control through rigging and motion generation metrics. Evaluation combines programmatic measurements of geometry, motion, and numeric constraints with rubric-based visual scoring by multimodal language model. Rigging. Rigging evaluation metrics include Source Fidelity, J2J, mIoU, Joint validity, Edge p99, and Rigid RMS. Source Fidelity measures the proportion of valid rigs that keep the source mesh, while J2J and mIoU measure jointposition error and skinning segmentation agreement against manually designed ground truth. Joint validity measures the fraction of joints inside or near the mesh surface. Edge p99 and Rigid RMS measure edge-length changes under standard poses and non-rigid distortion of mechanical parts, respectively. All are computed programmatically. Motion. Motion evaluation metrics include Semantic, Accuracy, Completeness, Morphology, Quality, Aesthetics, and Overall. Semantic assesses text instruction following against the scoring rubric, while Accuracy measures numeric constraint satisfaction programmatically. Completeness assesses phase order and completion through visual scoring for text tasks and programmatic checks for numeric tasks. Morphology and Aesthetics use visual scoring, with additional programmatic constraints on Morphology. Quality is computed from penetration, foot sliding, deformation, and smoothness tests. Scores are out of 100, and Overall is weighted score computed per case. Metric definitions and scoring details are provided in the supplementary material. 4. Using the rigs part mappings, the agent assigns motion to the relevant chains and end-effectors. Our end-effector operator instead bends whole chain by one scalar distributed through per-joint weights, so the agent shapes the motion of an entire chain of any length by adjusting only its end-effector trajectory through timed keys, contacts, and gait cycles, which supports complex motion on diverse chains. Rigging Evaluation Table 3 shows that equipping both agents with the Agentic Motion Framework makes them reliable at rigging raw assets, and the gains in Source Fidelity, J2J, mIoU, and joint validity are clearly visible. SkinTokens, UniRig, and RigAnything all process the input mesh, so their outputs differ from the source mesh that the rig must drive, which leads to their low Source Fidelity. Puppeteer keeps the mesh but still trails on J2J, mIoU, and joint validity. Edge p99 is essentially unchanged and Rigid RMS improves toward the best specialized value, so the gains do not come at the cost of larger deformation. Fig. 5 shows the skeletons predicted for nine-tailed fox and door in front, side, and top views. On the fox, the specialized methods produce sparse skeletons concentrated on the trunk and legs and leave most tails unrigged. GPT6.1sol alone places several chains outside the mesh, most visibly beyond the tails in the top view, and Claude-ops5.5 alone again misses most tails. With the Agentic Motion Framework, both agents grow separate chain into each tail while keeping the legs, head, and spine inside the body, and the skeleton stays consistent across all three views. On the door, the baselines draw diagonal bones across the panel or, in the case of UniRig, humanoid-like tree, whereas with the framework the agents place the main bone along the hinge edge and short bone at the handle, which matches the doors rigid articulation and explains the lower Rigid RMS. These gains come from multimodal observation. The agent labels each joint in the view where the part is clearest, such as the top view for separating tails and the side view for the legs, and the executor fuses these labels into 3D skeleton that follows the assets actual morphology rather than template. 5.3. Motion Generation Evaluation Table 4 shows that the three paradigms differ mainly in controllability. Specialized generators and video recovery produce plausible poses but rarely satisfy the ordered phases and numeric targets, since text segments or generated videos cannot impose required angle. Direct LLM generation can instead design motion according to the specified angles, but its results vary strongly across agents. The Agentic Motion Framework makes such angle-based design stable by attaching root orientation, joint rotations, and endeffector targets to key events in the program, and the table shows clear gains for both agents, especially in Accuracy, Quality, and Overall. The comparison also shows that direct LLM generation is very economical, and using our framework lowers its cost further. The supplementary material compares against variant without chain solving and against ArtiMo [58], whose articulation model is more restricted. To examine humanoid-specific motion generators, we compare MoMask, MotionBricks, and video-based recovery on the humanoid subset in Table 5. MoMask and the recovery methods still score below 26 overall even on this familiar morphology, showing that segment-level prompting and recovered video motion do not enforce the full instruction or its angles. MotionBricks deserves separate attention because it supports trajectory guidance. When Claudeops5.5 agent supplies structured IK targets and trajectories, it reaches 49.09 overall and leads all seven columns among the specialized generators. This large gain over MoMask shows that letting an agent plan trajectories while specialized module solves them is an effective division of labor, although MotionBricks itself remains limited to humanoid skeletons. Claude-ops5.5 + Ours follows the same division of labor, but supports arbitrary skeletons and controls rhythm through explicit phases and key events, raising the score further to 57.27 on the same subset. This supports separating parametric program authoring from deterministic execution. Fig. 6 shows key poses for two instructions. The humanoid must throw left punch, right punch, and spinning back kick in sequence within 2.2 s. Claude-ops5.5 + Ours raises its guard, throws both punches, turns its back during the spin, extends the leg backward for the kick, and recovers. Claude-ops5.5 without the framework produces unnatural poses with self-penetration. GPT6.1-sol + MoMask stays in guard and crouch poses with neither spin nor back kick, and GPT6.1-sol + DuoMo performs high kick and lunge but no punches. The two humanoid-specific pipelines thus each drop phase of the sequence. The scorpion must crawl half circle around target and stab toward the centre twice on the way. Claude-ops5.5 + Ours follows half-circle root path and lowers its stinger forward to stab. Claude-ops5.5 without the framework follows similar path, yet its stinger stays curled upward and never stabs, showing that direct generation can capture the global trajectory but loses the local part motion. The Seedance-based recovery and UniMate move the root only along short zigzag or hooked segment, and the body stays in place instead of circling the target. In both examples, explicit phase timing, root trajectories, and part targets in the motion program let the agent satisfy the global path and the local actions together. 5.4. User Study To verify the reasonableness of scoring with GPT6.1-sol, we conduct user study in which 30 volunteers rate each 8 result on Semantic, Completeness, Morphology, and Aesthetics for GPT6.1-sol + UniMate, Seedance 2.5 + Claudeops5.5, and Claude-ops5.5 + Ours. The subjective score averages all four dimensions for text tasks, and only Morphology and Aesthetics for numeric tasks, whose Accuracy and Completeness are computed programmatically. As shown in Fig. 7, the volunteer ratings follow the same trend as the LLM scores on both tasks and rank the three methods in the same order, confirming the reasonableness of the original scoring. 6. Conclusion We find that LLMs can already animate 3D assets directly from complex instructions, but not reliably. Rigging and complete multi-phase motion succeed only intermittently, with large variation across agents and morphologies. Existing benchmarks, built around conventional skeletons and simple prompts, do not expose this instability. DivDynBench closes that gap across six morphology categories. Comparing three LLM-based paradigms, we find specialized models efficient but skeleton-bound, video generation with motion recovery visually strong yet imprecise in timing and amplitude, and direct LLM-agent generation comparatively the most viable, though still unstable. Our Agentic Motion Framework, which couples agent-authored parametric programs with deterministic rigging and kinematics, markedly improves rigging quality and the controllability and stability of motion generation using the same base agents. We hope the benchmark and framework support the deployment of instruction-driven animation for diverse 3D assets.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) were used as generalpurpose writing assistants for this manuscript, performing language polishing and grammar checking through Codex, an LLM-based coding agent. They did not contribute to research ideation, method design, experimental implementation, data analysis, result interpretation, or the drafting of substantive content. All scientific content, claims, and conclusions were conceived and written by the authors, who reviewed every LLM-suggested edit and take full responsibility for the paper. The use of LLM agents as subjects of evaluation in our benchmark and framework is part of the research itself and is described in this paper.

Additional Results 9.1. End-to-end evaluation The main paper evaluates motion on provided reference rig so that motion scores are not entangled with rigging errors. Here we remove this separation, so the input is only the raw, unrigged mesh together with the motion instruction, and Claude-ops5.5 + Ours automatically runs the full pipeline from rigging to motion generation, after which only the resulting motion is scored. We evaluate on the humanoid, axial, and mixed-limb categories, which differ substantially in skeletal topology and body shape and are chosen to be representative. The same motion instructions and scoring are used, and only the rig source differs. Predicted rigs still yield solid results, with Overall scores of 49.80, 34.58, and 51.20 on the three categories, and Quality and Aesthetics stay close to the values obtained with the reference rigs. On mixed-limb assets, Overall (48.3351.20) is even slightly higher than with the reference rig, despite drop in Accuracy (48.3937.51). Our analysis suggests this relates to mixed-limb assets typically having outstretched limbs with little complex clothing or curling, body shape that is generally easier to rig accurately, and also because this is an end-to-end pipeline, rigging and motion generation are directly coupled, and this coupling may itself contribute to the Overall gain. These results suggest that our agent framework can carry out reasonably reliable end-to-end motion generation from raw mesh. 9.2. Ablation Study Fig. 8 (bottom-left and bottom-right of each case) further shows two ablations, Ours w/o chain solving and Ours w/o time separation, both compared against the full method at the top-left of each case. Chain solving distributes an end-effector target across the intermediate joints of the whole chain. Without it, the robots head likewise disintegrates briefly into particles during the turn, the long-tailed humanoids tail stays in nearrest, drooping shape throughout, neither wrapping the waist nor flinging out, and the legs adopt an unnatural, overly raised pose during the crouch phase of the standing backflip. These observations indicate that without solving the chain as whole, multi-joint parts struggle to reach the target shape required by the instruction and tend to show stiff or disintegrated intermediate poses. Time separation splits an instruction into an ordered sequence of phases that are then solved separately. Without it, the long-tailed humanoids tail alternates between an extended and drooping shape across frames, flinging toward the front before it has wrapped the waist, and the frame corresponding to the power-gathering phase of the standing backflip shows the arms thrown overhead, an action that does not belong to that phase. These observations indicate that without separating phases, the target poses may still be reached, but their order can be inconsistent with the phase structure of the instruction. 9.4.
